node.label: Linda Colley
node.date_label: Britons: Forging the Nation (1992) · Captives (2002) · The Ordeal of Elizabeth Marsh: A Woman in World History (2007)
node.description: A historian of Britain, empire and global connections. Her selected works move from the making of British identity to captivity and an individual woman’s transcontinental life. In her 2016 written interview she explains how captivity narratives can expose imperial weakness as well as power, provided they are embedded in other research. She describes Elizabeth Marsh as a way of writing global history through a woman’s constrained and mobile life, reconstructing her through dispersed sources rather than treating biography as an isolated portrait.

incident_edges.relationship: Uses Elizabeth Marsh’s itinerant life to investigate transcontinental connections and women’s place in global history.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Author’s answers on biography, missing letters and reconstructing Marsh through others’ writings. This identifies a specific biographical project, without treating one life as representative of every woman or attributing the book’s sources to Colley.

incident_edges.relationship: Colley values Bailyn’s Atlantic connections but challenges strong claims for their regional unity and the exclusion of early Asian connections.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Her 2006 review distinguishes praise for Atlantic inquiry from criticism of Bailyn’s stronger geographical model. The unity discussion at the end of section 1 and Asia discussion at the end of section 2 support this limited objection. Pestana’s book is separately reviewed; its claims are not silently assigned to Bailyn. No blanket rejection of Atlantic history or fresh reading of Bailyn’s whole 2005 book is asserted.

incident_edges.relationship: Colley praised Black’s documentation but sought an explanation of tourism’s effects on British self-understanding.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own review; final two paragraphs. Book unread. Praise and reservation coexist.

verification.note: Fresh selected publisher HTML: section 1 final paragraphs on Atlantic unity; section 2 final paragraphs on Asia and global connections. The review explicitly distinguishes its two books. Colley credits Bailyn’s contribution while objecting to his stronger claims of a discrete Atlantic whole. Her selected argument, rather than the unread whole of Bailyn’s 2005 book, supports the criticism. Full original HTML saved; no printed-page collation.
